short: The smallest build that tests the riskiest assumption — a learning device, not a small version of the product.
The document stating what will be built and why; increasingly displaced by lighter artifacts as build cost falls.
The stages software passes through from conception to retirement.
The product-side counterpart to the SDLC — discovery, definition, delivery, growth, sunset.
The agreed bar a work item must clear to count as complete — the place marketing readiness belongs if launches are to stop lagging.
A statement of intended sequence and rationale; degrades into a delivery schedule when outcomes stop being attached.
The ordered queue of not-yet-built work; its length is a measure of deferred decisions, not of ambition.
Treating customer contact as a weekly habit rather than a project phase, so evidence arrives before decisions rather than after.
Product manager, designer and engineering lead as the core discovery unit — balancing value, usability and feasibility, and omitting market context.
Building a throwaway probe to answer a question versus writing a document to predict the answer — the trade AI economics has shifted toward the spike.
Widening early discovery beyond the trio to test whether a proposed build addresses a real opportunity before solution design begins.
A checkpoint that work must pass before receiving further investment; only real if refusing is survivable under deadline.
The authoritative source for a given entity; whoever owns it owns the integration surface and, usually, the account.
The three routes out of a growth ceiling — reposition to an adjacent segment, add complementary value, or re-purpose the core for a new problem.
Large general-purpose models adapted to many tasks; the layer commoditising fastest, which is why positions rather than capabilities are becoming the differentiator.
Several specialised agents with distinct roles and handoffs, rather than one general agent asked to do everything.
The same input can produce different outputs, which breaks testing, support reproducibility and the user's ability to build a mental model.
When a capability appears in every competitor's deck it stops differentiating and becomes the price of entry.
The inverted sequence when building is cheap — produce something testable first, then judge it, rather than researching to a specification.
A durable advantage a competitor can't copy quickly; usually a position defended under pressure rather than a feature.
The specific benefit a defined buyer gets, stated in their terms — not a feature list and not a slogan.
A named, evidence-based sketch of a buyer or user, used to keep messaging and scope aimed at someone specific.
The organisational characteristics of the accounts you serve best — used to decide who to pursue and, more usefully, who to decline.
A one-page sales aid covering a competitor or objection; goes stale fast, which is why generating them is the classic automation candidate.
Equipping market-facing teams to articulate differentiation; a launch fails if reps can't say why the product is different.
The four phases across which go-to-market objectives, metrics and collateral all change — running one playbook across all four is how GTM falls out of sync.
How a product reaches and convinces a buyer — channel, message, pricing, enablement — and a design constraint rather than a post-build activity.
Deciding which capabilities sit in which tier; the guardrail is to gate the outcome, never the daily habit loop.
Framing a price against a reference the buyer already accepts, so the number is judged as a discount rather than a cost.
Structured review of why deals were won or lost; the richest source of positioning evidence and the most consistently neglected.
The category you ask to be evaluated in — which sets the comparison set and the price expectation before any feature is discussed.
Product marketers per product manager. 1:2 is the benchmark; 1:5 and beyond is where upstream work becomes arithmetically impossible.
How fast value moves through the funnel — opportunities × win rate × deal size ÷ cycle length. The metric that tells you whether enablement worked.
Feature usage falling within cohorts over time — an early signal of eroding fit that aggregate usage totals conceal.
Data that identifies a person, directly or in combination; the classification that triggers most regulatory obligations.
The traceable path of data from origin through transformation to use — the evidence base for both impact analysis and audit.
Naming a human accountable for a data asset's definition, quality and access; governance without it is documentation.
Automated collection of technical metadata from source systems — the ingestion problem underneath every catalog.
Labelling data by sensitivity so policy can act on it; useful in proportion to how precisely it drives enforcement.
Monitoring freshness, volume, schema and distribution to detect pipeline failures before consumers do.
Producing defensible proof that controls operated as claimed — the requirement that separates a governance product from a documentation tool.
Defining who may use which data under what conditions, and enforcing it rather than publishing it.
Decentralising ownership to domain teams who publish data as products, with federated governance holding the standards.
Treating a dataset as a product with an owner, consumers, a contract and a lifecycle rather than as pipeline output.
The EU regime setting lawful basis, subject rights and cross-border limits — the template most later privacy law follows.
California's privacy regime — opt-out rather than opt-in, with a broad definition of "sale" of personal information.

aka: Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados
short: Brazil's data protection law, closely modelled on GDPR — relevant to any product with Latin American customers.
Policy applied at the moment of access rather than reviewed afterwards — the difference between a control and a report.
The three exposures data governance is bought to reduce; they have different owners, different evidence and different tolerances.
A contract letting systems interoperate; in enterprise products the integration surface is often the product.
One authentication across many systems; in institutional sales it's a procurement precondition rather than a feature.
One tightly integrated system versus interchangeable parts behind contracts — a strategy choice about future optionality, not an IT preference.
Describing architecture at four zoom levels — context, container, component, code — which makes subjective requirements estimable and priceable.
Managed middleware connecting systems that were never designed to meet; the layer composable architectures depend on.
Government-facing interfaces for statutory reporting — non-negotiable, versioned on the regulator's timetable, and a moat for whoever implements them.
Deferred correctness and hardening that accrues interest; AI-accelerated generation increases the rate at which it is taken on.
Deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate and restore time — the standard four for delivery performance.
Bespoke configuration bought as flexibility that becomes a loan against future agility — every customisation is an upgrade you can't take.
Sequential delivery with sign-off between phases; still rational where change is genuinely expensive, and rarely where it isn't.
A time-boxed iterative framework with fixed roles and ceremonies; the most adopted and most cargo-culted agile method.
A fixed-length iteration ending in something potentially shippable; a forcing function for decisions, not merely a unit of scheduling.
The team's own review of how it worked; the only agile ceremony that changes the system rather than the plan.
Engineering-practice-led agility — pairing, TDD, continuous integration, collective ownership. The technical half Scrum usually omits.
Choosing when you cannot do everything; the skill becomes more valuable, not less, as building gets cheaper.
Deciding which problem is worth solving and how it's stated — the input that determines whether everything downstream matters.
The first willing users, chosen for enthusiasm rather than representativeness — which makes them the engine of internal change and a biased sample of the market.
Knowing which of several working solutions is the good one — the scarce human input once production is cheap.
When generation is cheap, verification becomes the constraint — and simultaneously the only remaining safeguard.
Whether a user can find a capability without being told it exists; the property conversational interfaces quietly discard.
Eliciting what the user actually wants rather than which control they pressed — the input problem natural-language interfaces inherit.
Whether a user can tell what the system just did and why; the requirement that replaces predictability once behaviour is generated.
Users learn where things are; interfaces that rearrange themselves intelligently discard a real form of acquired expertise.
Confidence exceeding reliability — the failure mode fluent output produces by default, and the reason calibration beats reassurance.
Fully loaded cost to win one customer; inflated by weak positioning long before it shows up as a marketing problem.
Total margin expected from a customer relationship; only meaningful beside CAC and only honest when churn is measured properly.
Normalised recurring revenue; useful decomposed into new, expansion, contraction and churn, misleading as a single figure.
Customers or revenue lost in a period; a lagging indicator of decisions taken several quarters earlier.
The share of signups reaching a defined first value; the definition is where most teams quietly measure setup instead.
Daily over monthly actives — a habit measure. High ratios indicate frequency, not value, and the two often diverge.
Randomised comparison of two variants; trustworthy only with adequate sample, a pre-declared metric and no peeking.
Grouping users by when they arrived and tracking each group separately — the only way early decay is visible before totals bend.
A lead scored on in-product behaviour rather than marketing engagement; the product-led counterpart to an MQL.
Metrics that move before an outcome versus after it; most dashboards are built almost entirely from the latter.
Numbers that rise reliably and inform no decision — usually cumulative totals, which can only go up.
Temporary support that lets a learner attempt something just beyond their current reach, then is deliberately withdrawn.
Scheduling review at widening intervals timed against forgetting — among the best-evidenced findings in learning science.
Game mechanics pointed at the learning objective rather than at engagement; the distinction decides whether it helps or distracts.
A structured path of advancing stages that gives the learner somewhere to be going, rather than a score to accumulate.
Gating new content behind demonstrated understanding, so progress is evidence of learning rather than of time spent.
Tuning challenge against ability so the learner is stretched but not stalled — too easy is boredom, too hard is abandonment.
The rate at which demand increases across a learning sequence; the parameter personalisation should adjust instead of removing the challenge.
Varying speed and sequencing to the individual learner while holding the standard constant.
Guiding a learner to an answer through questioning instead of supplying it — a product position with a real commercial cost.
A defensible teaching stance as competitive advantage — hard to copy not technically but organisationally, because holding it costs engagement.
The course-delivery platform — content, assignments, grades. Distinct from the student management system, which is the administrative core.
Australia's vocational sector — different regulator, funding and reporting from higher education, and a separate market.
The national identifier following an Australian learner across providers; a mandatory integration for anything touching enrolment.

aka: Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency
short: Australia's higher-education regulator; now requires institutional AI action plans, which makes AI governance a procurement gate.
The Australian government's student data collection; statutory, dated, and a large share of why SMS replacement is so risky.
TCSI's predecessor for higher-education reporting; still referenced in legacy integrations and institutional vocabulary.
The register of courses and providers permitted to enrol international students; compliance is existential for that revenue line.
The legislative framework protecting international students; drives reporting duties no product in the sector can opt out of.
In Australian education the government/non-government funding split predicts buying behaviour better than size or geography.
A market that looks national and behaves as separate jurisdictions with their own budgets and procurement — the org chart of the market is the GTM plan.
Upstream product marketing as an arithmetic problem; the five-agent system and the gate that makes it real.
Go-to-market as a repeatable production system — asset tiering, embedded virtual team, cadence locked to release.

term: The model is not the moat
short: Entering a crowded market on positions rather than capability; pedagogy and trust as non-commoditising differentiators.
Fit as perishable, with the data catalog's evolution as the worked case.

term: A product lens on the invisible
short: Making data risk operable; the catalog as the move that turns an invisible estate into a governable one.

term: AI product management: scarcity is gone
short: The operating model as a response to expensive engineering time, and what inverts when that constraint dissolves.

term: Agile in the age of AI
short: What remains scarce and human when iteration is nearly free.

term: Designing for a machine that can understand you
short: Interface as the place you steer and verify rather than operate; discoverability debt and trust calibration.
Wedge strategy in a structurally fragmented market; the org chart of the market as the go-to-market plan.

term: The core that won't sit still
short: Student management systems, composable re-architecture, and customisation as lock-in.

term: Personalising education without losing the human touch
short: Adapt the pace, protect the struggle; personalisation that supports a teacher rather than replacing one.

term: FitPulse — a pricing agent's first draft
short: Ready-made pricing exercise — value mapping, gating, risk, and where the agent's judgement runs out.
Turning conflicting enterprise requirements into one estimable product, using the C4 model.
Reusable game engines, a progression spine, and gamification pointed at learning rather than engagement.
A simulated GTM campaign — segmentation, message testing, KPIs by phase.
Responsible product thinking in a learning assistant — defer when uncertain, keep an adult in the loop.
The IAPP's AI governance certification — the credential that formalises the regulatory, risk and lifecycle vocabulary of the discipline.
The EU's risk-tiered AI regulation — obligations scale from minimal through limited and high risk to prohibited practices, with the tier determined by use case rather than model.
A voluntary US framework structured around four functions — Govern, Map, Measure, Manage — widely used as the operating skeleton for an AI governance programme.
The certifiable management-system standard for AI — the AI equivalent of ISO 27001, giving governance an auditable shape rather than a policy document.
Generic risk-management guidance; the vocabulary (likelihood, consequence, appetite, treatment) that AI-specific frameworks assume you already speak.
Structured documentation of a model's intended use, training data, evaluation results and known limitations — the disclosure artifact regulators increasingly expect.
The enumeration of every model and AI-enabled feature in an organisation; the AI counterpart of the data catalog, and the same precondition — you cannot govern what nobody can list.
Detecting when live inputs or model behaviour diverge from the conditions the model was validated against — decay in a form the accuracy metric may not show.
Establishing who answers for an automated decision, and how that answer is evidenced after the fact.
Explaining a specific output after the fact versus building a model whose mechanism is legible by construction — routinely conflated, with different regulatory weight.
Structured pre-deployment analysis of who an AI system could harm and how — increasingly a condition of approval rather than a courtesy.
The privacy assessment required where processing is likely to be high risk; the closest existing analogue to an AI impact assessment.
The principle that data collected for one stated purpose may not be quietly reused for another — the clause most often broken by training a model on existing customer data.
Documented origin and chain of custody for data — the question that decides whether a training set is defensible.
Australia's federal privacy regime and its principles governing collection, use, disclosure and access — currently mid-reform and diverging from the GDPR template in places.

aka: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner
short: Australia's privacy and freedom-of-information regulator — the body that investigates breaches and issues binding guidance.

Australia's prudential requirements for regulated financial entities covering operational risk and information security — the standards that make governance a board-level obligation in banking and insurance.

The federal voluntary principles covering human wellbeing, fairness, privacy, reliability, transparency, contestability and accountability — voluntary, but the reference point local procurement cites.
Adversarial testing of a model for harmful, biased or unsafe behaviour before release — increasingly named explicitly in regulatory guidance.
Building controls into architecture rather than layering review on top — the AI analogue of privacy by design, and the difference between a control and a report.
Unsanctioned use of AI tools inside an organisation; the governance problem that exists before any policy does, and the reason inventories are always incomplete.
Retrieving relevant source material and supplying it to a model at generation time, so answers are grounded in your corpus rather than in training data.
An open protocol for connecting models to tools and data sources through a common interface, rather than bespoke integration per system.
Further training a base model on task-specific examples to shift its behaviour — usually the wrong first move when prompting or retrieval would do.
How much text a model can consider at once; the constraint that shapes chunking, retrieval strategy and cost.
The unit models read and bill in — roughly a word fragment. The reason cost estimates built on word counts are wrong.
Numeric representations placing similar meanings near each other, enabling search by meaning rather than by keyword.
Storage optimised for nearest-neighbour search over embeddings; the retrieval half of most RAG systems.
Systematic measurement of model output quality against a fixed test set — the discipline that replaces 'it looked good in the demo'.
Constraints applied around a model to block unacceptable inputs or outputs — necessary because the model itself offers no guarantees.
Untrusted content carrying instructions the model then follows; the security failure mode with no clean fix, only mitigation.
Fluent output asserting things that are not true — the concrete mechanism behind the plausible-versus-correct gap.
Choosing model size, context length and call pattern against response time and unit economics — an AI product's central design tension.
Letting a model call defined functions to act rather than only describe — the mechanism that turns a chatbot into an agent.
Optimising to be the source a generative engine cites when it composes an answer, rather than a link someone clicks.
Near-synonym for AEO, emphasising the generative layer; both describe competing for citation rather than for ranking.
Optimising for retrieval and ranking in conventional search — still the substrate answer engines mostly retrieve from.
Low-substance pages produced at scale; discounted by search engines and, because assessment is partly site-level, capable of dragging down neighbouring pages.
Whether a page gives an answer engine a reason to name it — usually a worked example or a distinctive claim, never a restated definition.
Creating and capturing interest at scale; distinct from product marketing, and frequently confused with it in org design.
A lead judged ready for sales on marketing engagement signals; the metric most likely to be optimised at the expense of pipeline quality.
Top, middle and bottom of funnel — a content and channel taxonomy by buyer intent stage.
Assigning credit for a conversion across touchpoints; every model is wrong, and the choice of model quietly decides budget.
Staged communication moving a prospect toward readiness rather than asking for the decision immediately.
Your presence in category conversation relative to competitors; a leading indicator where brand precedes demand.
Defining a new category rather than competing in an existing one — high cost, high payoff, and usually claimed more often than achieved.
Long-run memory building against short-run measurable conversion; the allocation argument that recurs every budget cycle.
An enterprise qualification checklist — metrics, economic buyer, decision criteria and process, pain, champion — used to test whether a deal is real.
Someone inside the account who wants the purchase and will spend their own credibility on it; without one, the deal is a conversation.
The person who can actually release the budget, who is frequently not the person you have been meeting.
The early conversation establishing whether a real problem exists and who owns it — diagnostic, not a pitch.
Formal competitive procurement; usually written around an incumbent's capabilities, which is itself information.
The institutional purchasing process — security review, legal, vendor risk. Where most enterprise deals actually die.
Entering with a small deployment and growing inside the account; the commercial expression of a wedge strategy.
Addressing stated resistance; most objections are proxies for risk aversion rather than disputes about features.
Elapsed time from first contact to signature; the number that determines how much positioning has to do before sales begins.
The guided path from purchase to first value; the highest-leverage surface in the entire retention chain.
A structured account review with the customer; useful when it revisits their outcomes, theatre when it reviews your usage charts.
A composite predicting renewal likelihood; only as good as whether its inputs lead the outcome rather than describe it.
The recurring re-decision to keep paying; won or lost months earlier, in onboarding and in whether value was reached.
The deliberate play that grows an existing account — seats, tiers or modules — and the main engine behind NRR above 100%.
The agreed route for surfacing a failing account before it churns; its absence is why churn appears to arrive without warning.
Contribution per customer or transaction; whether growth compounds or consumes capital.
Total, serviceable and obtainable market — a sizing frame usually deployed to justify a decision already taken.
Net monthly cash consumption and the months remaining at that rate — the constraint behind most roadmap arguments.
Revenue less cost of delivery; the number AI inference costs are quietly eroding in products priced as pure software.
Accountability for revenue and cost of a business line — the step from senior product roles into general management.
The ability to raise price without losing volume; the cleanest available measure of whether a moat is real.
Whether to develop a capability or acquire it; decided by whether it is core to differentiation, not by cost comparison.
Whether an observed difference is distinguishable from noise; a threshold, not a measure of importance, and routinely read as both.
A trend that holds in every subgroup and reverses when the groups are combined — the reason aggregate results need segmenting before they are believed.
Extreme measurements tending toward average on repeat — which makes any intervention launched after a bad month look effective.
A third factor driving both the supposed cause and the effect; the reason observational wins so often fail to replicate in a controlled test.
A visible property suggesting how something can be used; the concept conversational interfaces discard wholesale.
How content and capability are organised, labelled and navigated — the structure discoverability depends on.
Revealing complexity only as needed, so novices are not overwhelmed and experts are not constrained.
The accessibility conformance standard referenced by procurement and, increasingly, by law — a gate rather than a nicety in institutional sales.
Assessment that informs ongoing learning versus assessment that judges the outcome; products conflate them and lose the feedback loop.
The band just beyond independent ability where support enables success — the target scaffolding and adaptive pacing aim at.
Effort that slows performance during practice and improves durable retention — the research foundation under protect the struggle.
The degree of genuine control a learner holds over path and pace; motivation depends on it more than on rewards.
A hierarchy of cognitive demand from recall to creation; useful for checking that assessment tests understanding rather than memory.
Reach, impact, confidence, effort as a prioritisation score — valuable mainly for exposing disagreement about the inputs.
Framing demand around the progress a customer is trying to make rather than their demographics — a discipline for finding the real competitive alternative.
The single measure a team aligns on as a proxy for delivered value; powerful when chosen well and distorting when chosen carelessly.
Goal-setting pairing a qualitative objective with measurable results; degrades into a task list when the results are outputs.
